formal_models.name: Runtime execution pipeline
formal_models.expression: source → JavaScript engine → execution frames/call stack → event loop/message processing → host APIs/I/O
formal_models.mechanism: The engine executes JavaScript inside a host runtime; the runtime supplies APIs and schedules messages.

formal_models.name: Event-loop processing
formal_models.mechanism: Messages are processed one at a time; each message runs to completion before the next is considered.

formal_models.name: Dynamic value typing
formal_models.expression: variable → value(type A) → reassignment → value(type B)
formal_models.mechanism: Type is associated with the value rather than the variable/expression.

formal_models.name: Operator-dependent coercion
formal_models.mechanism: Binary + may concatenate after string coercion, while - converts operands to numbers.

formal_models.name: Prototype delegation
formal_models.expression: object.property → own property? → prototype chain lookup → inherited method/property
formal_models.mechanism: Property lookup walks prototype relationships when a property is not directly owned.

formal_models.name: Lexical closure
formal_models.expression: outer lexical environment + nested function → retained internal state
formal_models.mechanism: A nested function retains access to outer bindings after the outer function finishes.

formal_models.name: Promise/async model
formal_models.expression: async operation → Promise → handlers / await → eventual result
formal_models.mechanism: Promises represent eventual results; async/await structures non-blocking asynchronous code.

formal_models.name: Browser security boundary
formal_models.expression: Web script → sandbox + same-origin policy + CSP → constrained execution
formal_models.mechanism: Browser restrictions limit system capabilities and cross-origin data access, while CSP constrains trusted executable content.

formal_models.name: XSS attack chain
formal_models.expression: attacker-controlled input → malicious script in target page → victim privileges → data/action compromise
formal_models.mechanism: The malicious script executes in the target application's security context.

formal_models.name: CSRF attack chain
formal_models.expression: attacker page → victim browser → authenticated target request → unintended state change
formal_models.mechanism: Cookie-based authentication can cause cross-site requests to carry valid credentials.

formal_models.name: ECMAScript standardization evolution
formal_models.expression: Netscape JavaScript → Ecma submission → ECMAScript editions → annual proposal process
formal_models.mechanism: Standardization moved from browser-specific implementations toward a shared evolving language specification.

formal_models.name: JavaScript/WebAssembly execution complement
formal_models.expression: JavaScript → performance-critical region → WebAssembly → same engine sandbox
formal_models.mechanism: WebAssembly complements JavaScript for performance-critical portions while remaining inside the engine's sandbox.

source_claims.claim: JavaScript is a core Web technology, alongside HTML and CSS, and conforms to ECMAScript.
Browsers contain dedicated JavaScript engines; engines are also used in servers and applications, with Node.js a major non-browser runtime.
Modern engines use JIT compilation and a runtime/event-loop model for non-blocking I/O.
JavaScript originated at Netscape in 1995 and was standardized as ECMAScript beginning in 1997.
ECMAScript 4 was mothballed; ECMAScript 5 emerged from a 2008 convergence and ECMAScript 6 arrived in 2015.
Node.js combined V8, an event loop, and I/O APIs, driving major non-browser JavaScript adoption.
JavaScript dominates client-side Web scripting and is widely used through libraries/frameworks.
JavaScript is dynamically and weakly typed, prototype-based, multi-paradigm, and supports first-class functions and closures.
Browser sandboxing and same-origin policy constrain JavaScript, while XSS, CSRF, prototype pollution, dependency risks, and browser flaws are security concerns.
JavaScript extends beyond browsers through Node.js, Electron, Cordova, React Native, Acrobat, GNOME Shell, and embedded systems.
Browser developer tools, linters, profilers, and benchmark tools support JavaScript development.
JavaScript influenced and was influenced by other languages/technologies and is complemented by JSON, transpilers, and WebAssembly.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: JavaScript is the language/ecosystem as used in practice; ECMAScript is the standardized language specification.
Despite name/syntax similarities, JavaScript is dynamically typed and prototype-based while Java is statically typed and class-based.
ECMAScript defines language semantics but not I/O; a runtime supplies networking, storage, graphics, and host APIs.
Dynamic typing concerns when/how types are associated with values; weak typing concerns implicit coercion across operations.
JavaScript's underlying inheritance remains prototype-based even when class/extends/super syntax is used.
The source states there is no distinct definition form; invocation context determines whether a function acts as a method via this.
The source describes JavaScript execution as single-threaded with queued messages and non-blocking I/O.
Promise is an asynchronous result abstraction; async/await is syntax for structuring asynchronous operations.
Sandbox limits system capabilities; same-origin policy limits cross-origin information access.
XSS executes attacker-controlled script in a target page; CSRF induces a victim browser to send an unintended authenticated request.
Client-side validation improves user experience but cannot be the sole security enforcement point.
Obfuscation can hinder inspection but does not make client-side code or embedded secrets confidential.
The source lists both but does not define a strict semantic boundary between them.
TypeScript is presented as a statically typed/strict language that transpiles to JavaScript.
WebAssembly complements JavaScript for performance-critical portions and runs in the same sandbox.
Vanilla JS means standard JavaScript without third-party libraries/frameworks.
Both use JavaScript engines, but their host runtimes expose different environment APIs.
The source contrasts Java's compiled-bytecode loading with JavaScript being loaded as human-readable source code.
var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped.
const prevents reassignment of the binding; the source does not state that referenced objects become deeply immutable.

misconceptions.misconception: JavaScript is Java.
misconceptions.correction: They are distinct languages with substantially different typing, object models, loading models, and histories.

misconceptions.misconception: ECMAScript and JavaScript are completely separate languages.
misconceptions.correction: JavaScript conforms to the ECMAScript standard; ECMAScript specifies the core language while hosts provide APIs.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic typing means JavaScript has no types.
misconceptions.correction: Types exist on values; variables can be rebound to values of different types.

misconceptions.misconception: Weak typing means JavaScript is dynamically typed.
misconceptions.correction: Dynamic typing and weak typing describe different properties: value-associated typing versus implicit coercion.

misconceptions.misconception: JavaScript inheritance is class-based underneath.
misconceptions.correction: The source states class syntax abstracts an underlying prototype inheritance mechanism.

misconceptions.misconception: const makes an object immutable.
misconceptions.correction: The source states const prevents reassignment of the binding; it does not define deep object immutability.

misconceptions.misconception: Client-side JavaScript can securely enforce validation.
misconceptions.correction: Client validation is convenience; security enforcement must also occur on the server.

misconceptions.misconception: Obfuscating JavaScript hides secrets.
misconceptions.correction: Client source can be extracted and obfuscation can be reverse-engineered.

misconceptions.misconception: CSP alone fixes all JavaScript security problems.
misconceptions.correction: CSP is one control; XSS, CSRF, dependency, browser, and sandbox issues remain distinct.

misconceptions.misconception: XSS and CSRF are the same attack.
misconceptions.correction: XSS executes malicious script in a target context; CSRF abuses a victim browser to make an unintended authenticated request.

misconceptions.misconception: JavaScript is single-threaded, therefore it cannot perform concurrent I/O.
misconceptions.correction: The event-loop model permits non-blocking I/O while messages are processed sequentially.

misconceptions.misconception: Web APIs are part of ECMAScript itself.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly separates ECMAScript language facilities from host-provided I/O and Web APIs.

misconceptions.misconception: WebAssembly replaces JavaScript.
misconceptions.correction: The source presents WebAssembly as complementary, especially for performance-critical portions.

misconceptions.misconception: Vanilla JS is a separate programming language.
misconceptions.correction: It is a term for using standard JavaScript without libraries/frameworks.

misconceptions.misconception: JavaScript only runs in browsers.
misconceptions.correction: It runs in Node.js, Deno, Bun, application frameworks, JVM contexts, and some embedded systems.

misconceptions.misconception: A function and a method are different language constructs in JavaScript.
misconceptions.correction: The source says the distinction occurs during invocation; method calls bind this to the receiver.

misconceptions.misconception: All JavaScript engines interpret source without compilation.
misconceptions.correction: Modern engines commonly use JIT compilation to improve performance.

misconceptions.misconception: Prototype pollution is ordinary prototype inheritance.
misconceptions.correction: Prototype pollution is a runtime vulnerability involving attacker modification of prototype properties.

misconceptions.misconception: Third-party package dependencies are automatically trustworthy.
misconceptions.correction: The source highlights stale, vulnerable, malicious, or removed dependencies as a supply-chain risk.

misconceptions.misconception: Browser sandbox bugs are only theoretical.
misconceptions.correction: The source cites historical cases where incorrect privilege handling enabled vulnerabilities.

historical_context.significance: Early popular graphical web browser preceding Netscape Navigator.
Netscape's browser became highly popular and hosted JavaScript.
Netscape hired Brendan Eich; LiveScript shipped in beta and was renamed JavaScript for the December release.
Microsoft's browser competition led to JScript and implementation divergence.
Started formal standardization leading to ECMAScript.
Market dominance and lack of cooperation contributed to ECMAScript 4 being mothballed.
Mozilla's Firefox helped break Internet Explorer dominance.
Jesse James Garrett coined Ajax with JavaScript as its backbone.
Google debuted Chrome with V8 and JIT performance.
Ryan Dahl created Node.js, expanding JavaScript outside browsers.
Major additions and refinements were formalized.
Ryan Dahl spearheaded a letter asking Oracle to free the JavaScript trademark.
